rashi:a3.1: At the beginning: at the beginning of the building one does not accept, since perhaps they intend to weaken [the builders’] hands.
rashi:a3.2: At the end: [a gift] to strengthen the Temple’s upkeep, where one cannot say [they intend] weakening of hands, is accepted. Another version: at the beginning, when the fear of the gentiles was not upon them, one does not accept; but at the end one accepts, out of fear. The first [explanation] is the main one, and this [second] is no reason, since all the days of the Second Temple the fear of the gentiles was upon them, and at its beginning more than at its end. And if you say that this “at the beginning” refers to the First Temple too: if so, what is the objection raised below from “And a letter to Asaph,” etc., which concerns the Second Temple?
rashi:a3.3: A defined item: one that is visible to the eye. One does not accept it from them, since it is a disgrace, and moreover they boast of it.
rashi:a3.4: A cubit, kalya orev: he mentions a cubit because we say in the last chapter of Menaḥot (107a): [One who says:] “Iron is upon me” may not give less than a cubit by a cubit, for the kalya orev. They would bring iron plates a cubit by a cubit, with tall spikes a cubit high fixed in them, and cover the top of the Sanctuary roof with them to drive away the ravens, so that they would not dwell there. Kalya means that it drives the ravens away, like the term in tractate Nidda (17a) for [a screen that] drives off flies, said of one who would drive the flies from his bed at the time of marital relations, for modesty, since relations are forbidden in the presence of any living creature. Another version: kalya orev, which holds back the ravens, as in “You will not withhold [tikhla] Your mercy” (Psalms 40:12).
rashi:a4.1: “And a letter to Asaph the keeper of the king’s park,” etc.: this was at the beginning of the building, and he was taking [materials for] Temple maintenance from Cyrus.
rashi:a4.2: Does not retract: since at the outset it intended good, it does not go back on it afterward.
rashi:a5.1: His pile: of his own grain.
rashi:a5.2: If he said: I separated it with the intent of Jews: that it should go wherever the teruma of Jews goes. Another version: that a Jew told him to separate it. The first is what I heard.
rashi:a5.3: It requires interment: and it is forbidden for benefit, since we are concerned that perhaps in his heart it was for Heaven, for consecrated property; therefore it is to be interred. And we are dealing with the present time, when consecrated property is forbidden for benefit [with no way to redeem it], as it is taught in Bekhorot (53a): One does not consecrate and does not valuate in the present time; and if one consecrated an animal, it is hamstrung; produce, clothing and vessels are left to rot.
rashi:a6.1: Yagod: he cuts off the place of the name and inters that piece, and uses the remainder, building it into the synagogue.
rashi:a6.2: For Heaven: for consecrated property; and in the present time it has no remedy.
rashi:a7.1: The reason is that the name is written on it: for then the matter is evident that in his heart it was for Heaven, since he wrote the name of the Holy One, Blessed be He, on it.
rashi:a8.1: A name not in its place is not sanctified: that is, only the place of the name is sanctified, and that piece is to be interred, while the rest is built into the synagogue, when he said: I separated it with the intent of Jews. Another version: a name not in its place, such as on beams and vessels, is not sanctified, since that is not its place; its place is only on parchment, with the verse written together with the name as it was given. But a name by itself is not in its place and is not sanctified. The first is what I heard, and it is the main one.
rashi:a10.1: To change it: for his own needs, and after a time he will repay.
rashi:a10.2: But for another: to lend it to his fellow, no. For himself one can say that he set it aside for charity on this condition, that if he needed it he would take it and repay another [coin]; but [lending it to] his fellow did not occur to him.
rashi:a11.1: They taught only: that he may change it, where he said: This sela is upon me for charity [Rashi’s wording joins “this” and “upon me”]. Since he said “upon me,” and accepted responsibility for it with regard to theft and loss, it is like his own.
rashi:a11.2: But if he said: This is: and did not say “upon me,” he must give [it as is].
rashi:a12.1: So that he should bear responsibility for it: since by using it he is like one who misappropriates a deposit, and it comes into his possession with regard to payment. But [where he] said “upon me,” he is liable for it in any case, so he should not use it.
rashi:a12.2: Rather, there is no difference: and it is permitted.
rashi:a13.1: Neither a vow is charity: since an unspecified vow is “The value of [this] is upon me for Temple maintenance.”
rashi:a14.1: Under “You shall not delay”: and this is the meaning: charity is a vow, in that it stands under “You shall not delay,” like a vow, as is said in the first chapter of Rosh HaShana (6a): “With your mouth” (Deuteronomy 23:24): this is charity.
rashi:a15.1: This halakha: that of one who says: This sela is for charity, etc.
rashi:a15.2: You teach it this way: that Rav Naḥman said “it is permitted to change it” without specification, and Rabbi [Davidson: Rav] Ami explained it as whether for himself or for another, and Rava then explained it as whether [he said] “upon me” or “this is.” We teach it explicitly, etc., and the whole explanation is in the words of Rav Naḥman.
tosafot:a1.1: It was taught in one baraita: a gentile who pledged a gift for Temple maintenance: The reason he does not establish [the two baraitot] as [a dispute of] tanna’im, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir [above, 5b], in a case where there is no weakening of hands, such as [a gift] from the king, is that if so, he should not have said “one accepts” and “one does not accept”; rather, he would need [to say] “it is sanctified” and “it is not sanctified.”
tosafot:a1.2: It was taught in one baraita: a gentile who pledged a gift for Temple maintenance, one does not accept from him, etc.: And if you say: let him answer that this is Rabbi Meir and that is Rabbi Yehuda; one can say that if so, he would need [to say] “it is sanctified” and “it is not sanctified.” [Saying] one does not accept it from him for Temple maintenance implies that it is sanctified, and it implies that both [baraitot] hold like Rabbi Yehuda.
tosafot:a2.1: This at the beginning, that at the end: Rashi explained: at the beginning, weakening of hands applies, and at the end, weakening of hands does not apply. And our teacher further explained: at the beginning, at the start of the building, there is reason to fear that they might later go back and contest, saying: We have a share in the Temple. At the end, a defined item is not accepted, lest it serve them for a name and for glory; an item that is not defined is accepted, since contesting no longer applies once the Temple has already been built. This also explains well what is said shortly: the government is different, since it does not retract, and there is no fear of contesting.
tosafot:a3.1: Such as a cubit kalya orev: the Arukh explains, in these words: Since in the First Temple its sanctity was [felt] by the whole congregation, and the Divine Presence rested in it, birds would not fly over it. But in the Second Temple they feared, since its sanctity was not like the sanctity of the First, that birds might fly over the Sanctuary and drop something impure there. So they made a figure to scare the birds off the Sanctuary roof, and called it kalya orev, that is, this keeps the ravens from flying over the Sanctuary roof. It is a figure like those that crop-watchers make now. End of his words. Some object: it says in Mo’ed Katan (9a), regarding Solomon, that he should have left out the cubit of the kalya orev, and it answers that the cubit kalya orev is a need of the building; evidently it existed in the First Temple. One can say that Solomon feared that perhaps [the Temple] would not have sanctity, and when they saw that it was holy, they removed it.
tosafot:a4.1: They raised an objection: “And a letter to Asaph the keeper of the park”: “And this was at the beginning of the building, and he was taking Temple maintenance from Cyrus.” So says the Kuntres [Rashi]. This does not seem right, since the whole building was from Cyrus, and there are several verses [about it]; it is also written: “And that which they have need of, young bullocks, and rams, and lambs” (Ezra 6:9). It seems to me that certainly they were not particular about that, since it was by decree, and through Isaiah [it was said]: “He shall build My city” (Isaiah 45:13). But Asaph the keeper of the park was far from Cyrus and not truly his; rather, [the king] decreed that they give for the needs of Temple maintenance, which was imposed on them, since he ruled over the whole world. In this there is room for concern, either of weakening of hands or of contesting, as I explained.
tosafot:a5.1: If he said: I separated it with the intent of Jews: This implies that a gentile is [subject to the law of] teruma for his own [produce], and so it is implied in the second chapter of Gittin (23b). And what is said in Zevaḥim, chapter Beit Shammai (45a), that he is not [subject to] teruma for his own, is no difficulty, since it is a dispute of tanna’im, [cited] in the second chapter of Kiddushin (41b), as we learned: The teruma of a gentile renders [ordinary produce] a mixture, and one is liable for the [added] fifth for it; and Rabbi Shimon exempts.
tosafot:a6.1: He cuts it off and uses the remainder: This implies [that he may use the rest] by cutting the beam, and not benefit from that piece opposite the name, since in its own place, at least, the name sanctified [the wood]. And one must be careful, when writing a Torah scroll or tefillin and scraping away the place of the name, not to write [something else] in its place.
tosafot:a14.1: While charity, it is permitted to use it: He understands that it deals with both “this” and “upon me.” And so the ruling is like Rav Naḥman: one who says: This sela is for charity, may change it, whether for himself or for another, whether he said “upon me” or “this.” And “to change it” means to borrow it.
tosafot:a16.1: As long as it has not come into the possession of the charity collector, it is permitted to change it: Rabbeinu Barukh explained “permitted to change it” literally, [to use it] for another mitzva: if a person vowed a sela as charity for the poor, he may do another mitzva with it as long as it has not reached the collector. But the expression “to change it” does not imply this. So I found written in the Tosafot of Rabbi Moshe of Évreux, from the writing of his brother; and he explained that “to change it” does not mean for another mitzva, since above it says “permitted to change it, whether for himself or for another,” which means to borrow it. Moreover, from what is said, “But Rabbi Yannai borrowed,” it implies that it is speaking of borrowing. Therefore it seems one should say that it is speaking of borrowing; but to change it [to another purpose] is certainly forbidden even when it has not come into the collector’s possession. It speaks of borrowing, and once it has come into the collector’s possession, it is forbidden to borrow it. And what is said in the first chapter of Bava Batra (8b), “The townspeople may turn the [charity] fund into the soup kitchen,” is with the permission of the townspeople, but the collector himself is forbidden. And the Ri says that there they may change it even not for a matter of mitzva, as long as it is for communal needs. And one must be careful not to borrow the town’s charity money once it has reached the collector, even with the permission of the community, since this is not a communal need. So I found written.
tosafot:a16.2: In brief: The prohibition once it reaches the collector applies only to an individual; the townspeople may change it, as Bava Batra (8b) implies: the townspeople may turn the fund into the soup kitchen and the soup kitchen into the fund, and change it for whatever they wish, but only for a matter of mitzva, as is said at the end of this passage (6b) about a Jew who donated a candelabrum or a lamp to a synagogue. What is said in Bava Metzia (78b), that a Purim collection is for Purim and a town’s collection is for that town, and outside the town it is forbidden to change it, speaks of the collector. By this reasoning Tosafot settles Bava Kamma (36b): a man who struck his fellow was told to give him half a zuz; [the victim] said, since it is only half a zuz I don’t want it, let it go to the poor; then he said, I will go and restore myself with it; and Rav Yosef told him the poor had already acquired it. Tosafot asks how he could have retracted even had the poor not acquired it, since Rosh HaShana (6a) says “With your mouth: this is charity.” Answer: he wanted to borrow it and repay later, and Rav Yosef told him that since it had come into his hand and he was [as] the collector, it was forbidden to change it. Alternatively, he thought it was not charity at all since [the poor] had not taken hold of it, and Rav Yosef taught that the poor acquired it, as in a transfer made in the presence of all three. gershom:a1.1: This at the beginning, that at the end: if at the beginning he said: I wish to donate, we tell him that we do not accept it; but if he [already] donated, we accept it, and that is “at the end.”
gershom:a2.1: Even water and salt: which are certainly meant for sale and will not be visible in the building; even so, one does not accept.
gershom:a3.1: A defined item: one that is visible in the building is not accepted [from them], because of “not for you and for us” [to build; Ezra 4:3]; and moreover, lest he regret what he vowed and want it returned to him. But an item that is not defined and is meant for sale is accepted from them. And this “cubit kalya orev” means: this and anything like it that is a visible item.
gershom:a4.1: That he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the castle: evidently one accepts a defined item from them.
gershom:a5.1: The government is different, as it does not retract: once it has given, we do not fear that it will ask for it to be returned to it, as Shmuel says, etc.
gershom:a7.1: If he said: I separated it with the intent of Jews: I want it to be done with it as a Jew does; it is given to a priest.
gershom:a8.1: Perhaps his heart was toward Heaven: perhaps he separated it with this intent, that it should have the sanctity of the Most High, for example that a burnt offering be bought with it, which is entirely for the Most High, and he does not want a priest to eat it.
gershom:a9.1: And the [holy] name is written on it: beforehand.
gershom:a10.1: Yagur [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads yagod]: he cuts off from the beam the place of the name, and uses the remainder for the needs of the synagogue.
gershom:a11.1: Perhaps his heart was toward Heaven: as we said, and not that a person should benefit from it.
gershom:a12.1: And this teaches us: that is, it was needed to teach us [the case of the name] because of the first clause, since it contains a novelty.
gershom:a13.1: A name not in its place: not in the place fit to write it, such as in a book or a place of honor, is not sanctified, as we learned, etc.
gershom:a14.1: It is permitted to change it: to borrow it for his needs and repay it after a time.
gershom:a15.1: It was understood from this: for himself it is permitted to borrow it, since he will not delay it, as he himself consecrated it; but for another, no, since [the other] does not care and will delay it.
gershom:a16.1: They taught that it is permitted to change it only where he said “upon me”: since he became liable for responsibility for it, he will certainly repay it.
gershom:a17.1: So that he should bear responsibility for it: which amounts to benefit from consecrated property.
gershom:b1.1: Rather, there is no difference: whether he said “upon me” or said “this,” it is permitted to change it.
gershom:b2.1: Charity is like a vow, so that one transgresses “You shall not delay” with regard to it.
gershom:b3.1: But Rabbi Yannai: who was a collector, borrowed for himself and repaid, even though it had come into his hand.
gershom:b4.1: As the longer he leaves it: since he cannot repay it, and there is nothing in the charity purse, he impels the public, [telling them] there is no charity in it, and he brings the poor more than he owes the purse; it is a benefit for the poor, and in the end, when he had [the money], he would repay it. But anyone else is forbidden to change it once it has come into the collector’s hand.
gershom:b6.1: No difference for a matter of mitzva: even for redeeming captives.
gershom:b7.1: Before its owner’s name has been forgotten, it is prohibited to change it: (and the reason [applies to] a gentile, when [the name of] its owner has not been forgotten) since people remember who consecrated it and say: This is the candelabrum of so-and-so.
gershom:b8.1: Even a Jew too: as long as its owner’s name has not been forgotten, it is prohibited to change it.
gershom:b9.1: And the reason is a gentile: as long as his name has not been forgotten from it, it is prohibited to change it even for a matter of mitzva, since a gentile screams: when he does not see it, he cries out and says: Where is the candelabrum that I consecrated?
gershom:b10.1: [Sha’azrak the Arab: a gentile merchant.] Raḥava changed it: for a matter of mitzva, before his name had been forgotten from it.
gershom:b11.1: As it was not common: since he was always away on his trading, and would not see it and would not scream; so it is like a case where his name has been forgotten from it.
gershom:b12.1: Sometimes he happens to come: and does not see it, and screams.
gershom:b13.1: Since he is not subject to setting and valuation: he cannot stand, since he is like a dead man, and it is written: “And he shall set… and he shall value.”
gershom:b14.1: Anything dedicated shall not be redeemed: that is, anyone who stands to be executed, his valuation is not redeemed, since he is not valuated.
gershom:b15.1: And according to Rabbi Ḥanina, who said he is valuated: even after the verdict.
gershom:b16.1: Due to the fact that one’s value is fixed: in the Torah, according to the years he has.
gershom:b17.1: That they give money and are atoned: as it is stated: “The ox shall be stoned, and its owner shall also be put to death,” a death at the hand of Heaven, and right after it: “If there be laid upon him a ransom.” Evidently those executed at the hand of Heaven have redemption.
gershom:b18.1: The verse states: “Anything dedicated shall not be redeemed”: one who stands to be dedicated, to be executed, has no redemption. Severe deaths, whose unwitting violation is not designated for atonement: such as the blasphemer and one who strikes his father or his mother.
gershom:b19.1: Lesser deaths, whose unwitting violation is designated for atonement: all the other capital offenses of the court. The verse states: “Anything dedicated,” to include both these and those.
gershom:b20.1: And does the first tanna say not? Does he say that he does not vow, valuate and consecrate?
gershom:b21.1: Rather, about these they do not disagree; they disagree only where he caused damage.
gershom:b22.1: A loan by oral agreement: and damages are like a loan by oral agreement, which is not like a full debt written in a document.
gershom:b23.1: A loan written in the Torah: damage, which is written in the Torah.
gershom:b24.1: Is like one written in a document: and he collects from the heirs.
gershom:b25.1: And there are those who teach it: this [statement] of Rav Yosef, who said a loan by oral agreement is collected, etc., with regard to this [baraita] of one taken to be executed.
gershom:b26.1: He cannot be brought back to stand before the court: since his verdict to be executed has been concluded, one does not go back and bring him before the court because he injured, since one does not delay his sentence; rather, once his verdict to be executed is concluded, he is executed [at once], because of the suffering of a living being [so as not to prolong his anguish].
rashi:b1.1: Rabbi Yannai: was a charity collector, and he borrowed the charity money for his own needs and repaid.
rashi:b1.2: As the longer he leaves it: as long as Rabbi Yannai has no money to repay, it is good for the poor.
rashi:b1.3: He impels: Rabbi Yannai [impels] the public, saying that he has no money to distribute to the poor, and presses them to [give] charity, and the poor gain.
rashi:b2.2: A lamp: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss) of silver or of gold.
rashi:b3.1: From what Rabbi Asi says, etc.: that is, since Rabbi Asi mentioned a gentile, who cries out and screams: Why did you change what I gave? By implication, with a Jew, who does not cry out, it is permitted to change it for a matter of mitzva. For if with a Jew it were forbidden, why would he need to mention a gentile?
rashi:b3.2: Before its owner’s name has been forgotten: from it, since people still say: This is the candelabrum donated by so-and-so the gentile.
rashi:b3.3: It is prohibited to change it: since he screams.
rashi:b4.1: With regard to what: does Rabbi Asi say that it is prohibited to change it? If we say, etc.
rashi:b7.1: Not common: for Sha’azrak to be in town to scream, since he was a merchant who traveled around the towns.
rashi:b8.1: MISHNA: One who is moribund and one who is taken to be executed, etc.: the Gemara explains the reason.
rashi:b8.2: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya: disagrees about one taken to be executed, but about the moribund he agrees, since it is written: “Then he shall be set… and [the priest] shall value him” (Leviticus 27:8), and one who is moribund is not subject to setting and valuation.
rashi:b8.3: That one’s value is fixed: in the passage of valuations. But about [being the object of] a vow he agrees [that he is not vowed], since [then] one must assess him as [a slave] sold in the market, and this one is not sold in the market, that is, no one would buy him and lose his money.
rashi:b8.4: He vows and valuates, etc.: the Gemara explains what Rabbi Yosei comes to say, since the first tanna did not say “he does not vow,” such that if he said: The value of so-and-so is upon me, he would be exempt; he said only “he is not vowed.”
rashi:b9.1: GEMARA: But why is he not valuated? His value is fixed.
rashi:b10.1: Anything dedicated shall not be redeemed: one who is fit to be dedicated [ḥerem] and executed is not included in redemption.
rashi:b12.1: For those executed at the hand of Heaven: such as what is written: “The ox shall be stoned, and its owner shall also be put to death.” And one cannot say that this death is at the hands of man, since we say in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (15b): “He that struck him shall surely be put to death; he is a murderer” (Numbers 35:21): for his own murder you execute him, but you do not execute him for the killing done by his ox.
rashi:b13.1: Whose unwitting violation is not designated for atonement: such as the blasphemer and one who curses his father, for if he did it unwittingly, there is neither an offering nor exile.
rashi:b13.2: Lesser deaths: that is, lesser for this matter, in that their unwitting violation is designated for atonement, such as a murderer, whose unwitting [killing brings] exile, and an idol worshipper, one who desecrates Shabbat, and one who engages in forbidden relations, whose unwitting [act brings] a sin offering.
rashi:b15.1: Everyone agrees: certainly his vow is a vow and his consecration is consecration, and he valuates others, since he is a person of understanding.
rashi:b16.1: A loan by oral agreement: such as this one, who caused damage and did not stand trial for it before his death. [On Rava’s line:] Payment for damage is written in the Torah, and by Torah law [his property] is bound to it even against his will.
rashi:b18.1: And there are those who teach it: this [dispute] of Rav Yosef and Rabba [Davidson: Rava].
rashi:b18.2: He is liable: since he is a person of understanding.
rashi:b18.3: They are exempt: since he has no value, and he stands to be injured [in any case]. And all these [cases] speak of one to be executed under the laws of Israel.
rashi:b18.4: To be brought back to stand before the court: you cannot bring him back to the court to stand trial for what he injured, since one does not delay his sentence.
tosafot:b4.1: If you say for a voluntary matter, why specifically a gentile? Even a Jew too: he could equally have said: why specifically before its owner’s name has been forgotten? Even once it has been forgotten too.
tosafot:b10.1: From where [is it derived] that one taken to be executed who said: My valuation is upon me, did not say anything: And it cannot be excluded [merely] because he has no monetary value, for above (Arakhin 2a) the repulsive and one afflicted with boils were included [in valuations].
tosafot:b15.1: When they disagree, it is where he caused damage: And where he consecrated they do not disagree, since as soon as he consecrated, the consecration takes effect, and it is not like a loan. But one can ask: why do they not disagree where he vowed or valuated? One can answer: he mentions “caused damage” because [the mishna] teaches “liable” [to payment] about causing damage, which implies that they disagree about causing damage alone; and with vowing and valuating, perhaps [the obligation] takes effect at once, and then [the Temple] collects from the heirs. And “he vows and valuates” was needed, since you might have thought that since he is not vowed and not valuated, he also does not vow or valuate; it teaches us that he vows, valuates and consecrates like other people.
